title: MoneyMente
l1d: Everything starts with knowing where your money goes. A simple guide: half for needs, thirty percent for wants, and twenty percent for saving and paying debt.
l2d: Before attacking debt, build a small cushion of one thousand dollars, or one month of expenses if that is lower, so surprises do not push you back into debt.
l3d: Put every extra dollar on your debts. Snowball pays the smallest balance first for quick wins. Avalanche pays the highest interest first and usually saves the most money.
l4d: Grow your cushion to three months of expenses. This is your safety net if you lose income.
l5d: Give every goal a target, a date and a monthly amount. A goal is on track when your plan reaches the target in time.
l6d: With a safety net and no costly debt, you can start investing. Beginners often choose low-cost diversified index funds, add money every month, and think in decades, not days.
l7d: Time is your biggest ally. Move the sliders to see how monthly contributions grow with compound interest.

disc: Educational purposes only. This is not financial advice.

tip1: Pay yourself first: move money to savings on payday, before you spend.
tip2: Keep your emergency fund in a separate account so you are not tempted to spend it.
tip3: Never skip a minimum payment: late fees and penalty rates make debt grow faster.
tip4: Only real emergencies count. A sale is not an emergency.
tip5: Wait 24 hours before any big purchase. Most urges fade.
tip6: Never invest money you will need within five years, and avoid anything promising guaranteed high returns.
tip7: Raise your monthly contribution whenever your income rises. Small raises add up over decades.

q_cta: Answer 5 quick questions to determine your Financial Health Score.
q_save_q: 1. Saving habit: How consistently do you save part of your income each month?
q_save_0: Rarely or only when money happens to be left over
q_save_50: Save manually in most months (5–15% of income)
q_save_100: Automate saving 20%+ every payday (pay yourself first)
q_run_q: 2. Safety net: If your main income stopped today, how long could cash savings cover essentials?
q_run_0: Less than 1 month (would rely on credit or borrowing)
q_run_50: 1 to 2 months of essential expenses saved
q_run_100: 3+ months in a dedicated emergency fund
q_debt_q: 3. Debt control: How do you manage credit cards and loans each month?
q_debt_0: Carry high-interest debt and pay only minimums
q_debt_50: Pay on time and add extra toward debt balances
q_debt_100: Debt-free or pay credit cards in full every month
q_bal_q: 4. Spending & bills: How well do your monthly expenses fit your income (50/30/20)?
q_bal_0: Often overspend or don't track monthly expenses
q_bal_50: Pay all bills on time and roughly break even
q_bal_100: Needs ≤50%, Wants ≤30%, track spending every month
q_inv_q: 5. Future & investing: Do you invest and plan ahead for future-year expenses?
q_inv_0: Not investing or planning annual expenses yet
q_inv_50: Starting small investments & planning 1 year ahead
q_inv_100: Investing monthly + multi-year goals & expense reserve

score_source: Your score combines your entered financial figures with your answers below. The five categories and their weights are shown here.
score_weights: Weights: saving rate 25%, emergency runway 25%, debt load 20%, budget balance 15%, investments 15%. Financial figures are combined with your answers after you finish the questionnaire.

plan_debt_d: You listed {n} in debt. Review the highest rate first ({r}% APR), while keeping every required minimum payment current.
plan_reserve_d: Build toward a cash reserve of about three months of budgeted expenses; the remaining gap is {n}.
plan_goals: Adjust a goal that is behind schedule
plan_goals_d: “{g}” needs about {n} per month under the current estimate. Revisit the target, date, or contribution.
plan_invest_d: Your basic cash reserve is in place and no debt is listed. Compare risks, fees and time horizon before investing; returns are not guaranteed.
plan_maintain_d: Your listed basics look covered. Revisit your budget, reserve and goals when your situation changes.

Similarity is a weighted average of 9 answers: sex, age, area, education level, household type, marital status, department, municipality and languages. Age tolerates up to 20 years apart. Occupation and career goals are not part of the calculation.

pf_advisor_note: Buck's chat already receives your numbers. With the profile (age, household, occupation, department) it could give more tailored advice. For example, a single-parent household needs a larger emergency fund than a couple without children, and someone aged 55 prioritizes retirement more than someone aged 25.
